Notes from course #3 of my Claude Certified Architect track: Claude Platform 101. See previous: Claude Code 101
Press enter or click to view image in full size

I was three slides into the MCP section when I stopped in my tracks. Not because the slide was confusing. Because it made something click that eighteen months of building agents on Copilot Studio hadn’t quite named for me. For the longest time I was confused between Agent Tools vs MCP and MCP vs APIs. This concept finally put that to rest:
tools for your data, skills for your process, MCP for third-party services.
Every time I’ve had to decide whether to write a custom connector or reach for an existing integration, whether to hard-code a procedure or hand Claude a checklist and let it reason — I was making an architecture decision without a framework. Now I have one.
Here’s what stuck from this module, and why.
Claude Development Platform in a nutshell
The Claude Developer Platform is Anthropic’s infrastructure for building with Claude programmatically: a REST API, SDKs, CLIs, and a console for keys, usage, managed agents, and prompt testing.
The platform breaks into primitives, infrastructure, and controls.
Primitives
Primitives are the raw material — the Messages API, tool use, files, web search, code execution, MCP, skills.
Infrastructure
Infrastructure is what you build on top when you stop wanting to babysit a loop yourself — managed agents, retries, queues, observability.
Controls
Controls are how you know any of it is working — dashboards, evals.
Press enter or click to view image in full size

Build with primitives. Scale on infrastructure. Run with control.Build with primitives. Scale on infrastructure. Run with control. It’s a clean enough line that I’ve already started using it to explain our agent portfolio to stakeholders who don’t want the technical weeds — just the shape of the thing.
Tools vs. Skills vs. MCP — is it all the same?
This is the one I keep coming back to, because it’s the one I’ve gotten wrong repeatedly in meetings.
Press enter or click to view image in full size

Tools (Custom & Built-in server tools & Client tools)
A tool is a function you define and expose to Claude so it can connect to your systems — your database, your proprietary API.
Tools are JSON schemas with three parts: a name, a description, and an input schema. The description is what Claude reads to decide whether to call the tool. Claude doesn’t execute the tool — your code does.
SDK’s tool runner takes functions, reads types and docs to build the schema for you and handles the entire tool use/tool result loop internally
Types of tools:

• Anthropic runs Server tools (web search, code execution, web fetch) server-side and hands you the finished response. There’s no agent loop and no stop_reason. The response has new block types.

• Client tools run where your code runs. They’re shipped in the Claude SDK, so you don’t have to define the schema yourself. (eg. Memory — Claude reads and writes memory across sessions, Bash — a persistent bash shell so Claude can execute commands)
Skills
Skills are folders of instructions (SKILL.md file), scripts, and resources that teach Claude a procedure — your report template, your review checklist. Instructions, not integrations.

• Skills load progressively. Only the name and description load at startup; the full Skill loads into context when the agent decides to use it.

• Upload once with client.beta.skills.create, then attach with container.skills on any messages.create call — a list, so you can layer multiple Skills.

• Pair with code execution when the Skill’s procedure needs to do real work.
Press enter or click to view image in full size

Tools vs. Skills: tools are about what Claude can do; Skills are about how you want it done.MCP
MCP connects Claude to someone else’s service, and they maintain the integration.
Each server exposes its own tools — with descriptions, schemas, and authentication — through a standard protocol. When their API changes, they update their server. You change nothing.
Claude introspects the server, gets the list of tools and their schemas back, and picks the right one for the prompt.

• Declare the connection in mcp_servers (type, URL, name, optional auth token) and grant access with an mcp_toolset entry in tools.

• Scope down access by setting default_config: {"enabled": False} and enabling specific tools in configs — handy for keeping a server read-only.
Visit modelcontextprotocol.io for the list of available servers and to learn more about the protocol.
The Anatomy of a Request
Every API call goes through the messages.create function which gives you full control over:
1. Model — which Claude model handles the request
Anthropic offers three model tiers: Opus for hard problems, Sonnet for daily work, and Haiku for volume.
Pro tips:

• Set up a simple evaluation — 20 or 30 representative examples

• Run the eval from Haiku upward and stop at the cheapest model whose output you’d actually ship. In production, route different tasks to different models inside the same endpoint instead of picking one model for everything.
2. Max tokens limit — a cap on how long the response can be
response.usage reports input and output tokens
3. List of messages
Objects with either user or assistant roles, structured similarly to how you'd have a conversation with Claude elsewhere. Add a system prompt to shape Claude’s behavior.
Here’s what that looks like in its most basic form:
import Anthropic from "@anthropic-ai/sdk";const client = new Anthropic();
const msg = await client.messages.create({
model: "claude-opus-4-7",
max_tokens: 1024,
messages: [{
role: "user",
content: "Hello, Claude",
}],
});
Pro tip:

• Store your API key in a .env.local file to keep it out of version control.

• The response content is an array of blocks — loop and check each block's type.

• Extended thinking is a feature that lets Claude reason step by step before responding. It generates visible internal reasoning tokens often called chain of thought then delivers answer. You can control how much claude thinks with the effort parameter — low, medium, high, xhigh, max
The agent loop, demystified
An agent is just: observe, decide, act, repeat. Claude requests a tool call, your code runs it, the result goes back, Claude keeps going. Stop when the stop reason is end_turn.
Press enter or click to view image in full size

What I hadn’t fully internalized before this course: you own the loop and the tools, Claude owns the reasoning. Managed agents exist for exactly the moment you don’t want to own the loop anymore — when a run would go too long, do too much, or need to survive a failure without you babysitting it. That’s a build-vs-buy call, and it’s the same call I make constantly deciding what stays in Copilot Studio versus what needs a pro-code layer.
Managed Agents
When you don’t want to own the loop, managed agents run this exact loop for you on Anthropic’s infrastructure. Claude Managed Agents is a suite of APIs for building and deploying agents at scale, hosted on Anthropic’s infrastructure. The building blocks are:

• Agents — definitions with specific tools, personas, and capabilities

• Sessions — individual runs you fire off from your own application

• Environments — sandboxes with the right packages and network controls. Sessions run in environments you configure, work in parallel, and stream tool calls back to your app in real time.

• Tools — including custom tools on your back end

• MCP — connections to services like Slack and Asana

• Memory — a store the agent reads before starting and writes to when done

• Outcomes — rubrics and graders that define and check what done looks like

• Multi-agent coordination — coordinators delegating to specialists
Things to note:

• The flow is: create an agent, create an environment, create a session, send events in, and stream events out.

• The agent (model, system prompt, toolset) is reusable across runs; the session is a single run; events are how everything flows.

• Open the event stream before sending your kickoff message — it only delivers events that occur after it opens.

• Watch for three events: agent.message (text), agent.tool_use (tool picks), and session.status_idle (done).

• Reach for managed agents when the loop would run too long, do too much, or need to survive a hiccup. Reach for a manual loop when you want full control.
To build an agent with Claude Code:
The built-in Claude API skill loads automatically when Claude Code detects the TypeScript SDK, or you can invoke it with /claude-api. Give it a prompt that names the file, the pattern, and the end state — it writes the code, runs it, and fixes errors in place. Claude API code follows a familiar shape: define a tool, hand it to a runner, return the result. Stub it, delegate it, review the diff.
Context management as four patterns, not one
Context is everything Claude sees on a turn. Once this finite window fills, the request fails.
Press enter or click to view image in full size

Just-in-time context, server-side compaction, prompt caching, the memory tool. Anthropic frames these as four tools you layer together in production rather than four competing approaches you pick between. That reframe is useful on its own — I’d been treating caching and memory as separate problems to solve, not as pieces of the same context budget.
Press enter or click to view image in full size

• Just-in-time context: load what’s needed now, let tools pull in the rest. This is the design pattern of the four.

• Server-side compaction: add a context_management key, and the API summarizes old turns automatically when input crosses the trigger threshold.

• Prompt caching: mark stable parts of the request and reuse them across calls at a fraction of the cost.

• The memory tool: Claude reads and writes a memory directory via tool calls; you own the storage backend, so context survives across sessions.

Next up: the certification’s forth course: Intro to Claude Cowork. I thought the last course was a gold mine, this one unequivocally topped that. I wonder what the next one will bring.
